video_title: From Math Olympiads to Navier-Stokes: How Fast Is AI Progressing?
gist: Epoch AI's Greg Burnham argues benchmark data show smooth, on-trend AI progress even as models move from exams to solving open math problems (Erdos unit distance, Navier-Stokes), while continual learning, open-ended work and original concept creation remain gaps; he flags recursive self-improvement and cyber thresholds as the discontinuity risks.

insights.claim: Epoch's Epoch Capabilities Index, which stitches S-curve benchmark scores together statistically, shows frontier AI capability rising roughly linearly across model generations with no slowdown on any measure Epoch tracks.
insights.speaker: Greg Burnham (Epoch AI)
insights.so_what: Bearish-on-progress narratives (plateau) lack support in the aggregate benchmark data.
insights.quote: we really do see this thing continuing to go up uh you know pretty smoothly linearly

insights.claim: Benchmarks repeatedly go from near 0% to ~100% within one to two years, forcing constant creation of new benchmarks; this has been the story of at least the last three years.
insights.speaker: Greg Burnham (Epoch AI)
insights.so_what: Saturation of any given eval is the norm, so eval-based moats and static benchmarks lose signal fast.

insights.claim: The linear aggregate trend arises because new models (Opus 4.5/4.6/4.7, GPT 5.2/5.4) improve on all benchmarks at once; Burnham flags the linearity as partly a statistical artifact of stitching sigmoids and says reasoning models around late 2024 may have raised the slope.
insights.speaker: Greg Burnham (Epoch AI)
insights.so_what: Cross-benchmark correlation, not any single eval, is what drives the smooth trend; read single-benchmark jumps with care.

insights.claim: Two explanations for broad cross-benchmark gains: the 'shallow' one where labs collect targeted training data for each domain customers care about, and the 'deep' one where models generalize from math and software to domains never trained on; the mix is unclear and a large share of the industry is now rich training-data collection.
insights.speaker: Greg Burnham (Epoch AI)
insights.so_what: If deep generalization dominates, capability becomes hard to bound; if shallow dominates, data-vendor spend is the real driver.

insights.claim: Epoch's tests find nearly every new frontier release lands on trend with no trend breaks or accelerations; hyped launches are 'on trend, but the trend is crazy'.
insights.speaker: Greg Burnham (Epoch AI)
insights.so_what: Lab claims of step-function jumps are not showing up as discontinuities in the stats.
insights.quote: everything just about is on trend

insights.claim: Epoch's view is that AI progress is heavily mediated by raw inputs (GPUs, training compute, training data) more than algorithmic breakthroughs, so discontinuities in models should not appear until the compute and data supply chains ramp discontinuously.
insights.speaker: Greg Burnham (Epoch AI)
insights.so_what: Track compute and data supply chains as the leading indicator for capability jumps.

insights.claim: The main route to a discontinuity would be recursive self-improvement or a software-only intelligence explosion, where AI gets better at algorithmic innovation and does more with a fixed compute budget so the feedback loop no longer runs through the physical world; Burnham says on balance there is no evidence of this yet.
insights.speaker: Greg Burnham (Epoch AI)
insights.so_what: Watch for AI-driven algorithmic efficiency gains as the regime-change signal for AI progress.

insights.claim: Epoch is building a forthcoming test where offline AI models released just before a recent human AI-research breakthrough must improve the same efficiency metric without being told the innovation; so far models cannot replicate the human innovation.
insights.speaker: Greg Burnham (Epoch AI)
insights.so_what: Current models lack 'research taste' for AI R&D, which supports the claim that self-improvement is not imminent.

insights.claim: Burnham describes 'research taste' (deciding which experiment to run next and where to hunt for breakthroughs beyond more compute and data) as a capability AI does not yet show in AI R&D, though it is rapidly improving at adjacent skills; Epoch treats this as a tripwire for sudden capability uptick.
insights.speaker: Greg Burnham (Epoch AI)
insights.so_what: A crossing of this threshold would be the signal to expect faster-than-trend AI improvement.
insights.quote: there's this nebulous idea called research taste

insights.claim: As of fall 2024 LLMs still struggled with grade-school math (GSM8K); OpenAI's o1-preview then produced a huge spike on competition math, and by 2025 AI won gold on the International Math Olympiad and by early 2026 most original FrontierMath problems (advanced undergraduate to grad level) were solved.
insights.speaker: Greg Burnham (Epoch AI)
insights.so_what: Roughly a year and a bit took AI from hobbyist-high-schooler to competent grad-student math, illustrating how fast capability compounds once a training recipe (reasoning) works.

insights.claim: In May 2026 an internal model, probably like the publicly available Astra, solved the Erdos unit distance problem (how many points in a plane can be at unit distance from each other), a serious long-standing problem, by disproving a conjecture humans mostly believed true.
insights.speaker: Greg Burnham (Epoch AI)
insights.so_what: AI is now solving problems mathematicians independently care about, not just benchmark items.

insights.claim: An AI-assisted solution to the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem has recently been reported; OpenAI's reported system used a swarm of thousands of AI instances trying many approaches and sharing ideas, which Burnham says involves an element of brute force but at a higher level than before.
insights.speaker: Greg Burnham (Epoch AI)
insights.so_what: Parallel agent swarms are an effective scaling axis for hard reasoning, implying heavy inference-compute demand.
insights.quote: a swarm of thousands of different instances of AI systems trying lots of different things and sharing ideas

insights.claim: The Navier-Stokes solution appears to build on substantial prior human work; AI did not do ground-up theory building, which Burnham says is still not seen from AI.
insights.speaker: Greg Burnham (Epoch AI)
insights.so_what: Headlines overstate autonomy; AI currently excels at completing structured human groundwork.

insights.claim: Burnham says current AI has two edges on math: it has the literature effectively memorized and it is extremely patient and persistent with intricate, high-level logical computations; solutions so far have been unsurprising to mathematicians in hindsight, directions humans overlooked.
insights.speaker: Greg Burnham (Epoch AI)
insights.so_what: 'AI-shaped problems' (long intricate derivations plus broad background) are where AI will keep winning first.

insights.claim: AI-generated proofs are in the same form as human ones, and Burnham says that if a human had produced them they would be lauded for insightful connections across areas, so dismissing AI math as not impressive on human terms no longer holds.
insights.speaker: Greg Burnham (Epoch AI)
insights.so_what: Value is arriving in genuine research output, not just benchmarks.

insights.claim: What AI has not yet shown is inventing a new concept (analogous to the derivative or integral); Burnham notes this is rare even for humans, with about 90% of human math being proving or cross-applying existing ideas, so it may not be the first thing AI masters.
insights.speaker: Greg Burnham (Epoch AI)
insights.so_what: The next threshold to watch is concept creation, not problem solving.

insights.claim: Fields medalist Timothy Gowers did a post-hoc 'how big a hint' exercise on the unit distance solution: the hint 'look for a counterexample' plus one more piece would likely have let a human solve it, an example of Epoch's approach to assessing creativity.
insights.speaker: Greg Burnham (Epoch AI)
insights.so_what: Qualitative expert review suggests AI's win came from search in an under-explored direction.

insights.claim: Epoch's newest FrontierMath sets consist of problems humans have tried and failed, in four interest tiers up to 'breakthrough'; none of the breakthrough tier is solved, and when a new model (Astra) arrived it solved three new problems from the list.
insights.speaker: Greg Burnham (Epoch AI)
insights.so_what: Unsolved-problem benchmarks with auto-verification are the new frontier eval, and the breakthrough tier is a clean marker for the next jump.

insights.claim: Measuring AI on open problems is a phase transition in capability measurement because answers are not known in advance; Epoch uses auto-verification techniques, and in scientific domains simply asks AI to beat the best human number on a metric, with optimization problems always remaining a usable benchmark.
insights.speaker: Greg Burnham (Epoch AI)
insights.so_what: Eval design now relies on metrics that can be checked cheaply, which favors quantifiable domains first.
insights.quote: optimization is uh is always going to be a benchmark even if we're superhuman

insights.claim: Burnham says AI currently struggles to judge how close it is to a solution on partial progress; giving models more thinking time on problems where they made partial progress produced nothing so far.
insights.speaker: Greg Burnham (Epoch AI)
insights.so_what: Weak self-assessment limits autonomous research loops.

themes.theme: Where AI still falls short: jobs and on-the-fly learning

insights.claim: Epoch's internal task tests find AI does well at literature summaries but is weak at compelling on-style visuals, new short data-driven insights, and proposing a new project and prototype; open-ended tasks remain 'a little meh' versus humans.
insights.speaker: Greg Burnham (Epoch AI)
insights.so_what: White-collar replacement is uneven: strong on retrieval and synthesis, weak on open-ended judgment and originality.

insights.claim: On Epoch's board game benchmark (Earthborne Rangers), models like GPT-5.6 score a level out of the box and stay flat across repeated playthroughs; GPT-6 scores much higher but also stays flat, still below top humans, so gains come across model generations, not from in-session learning.
insights.speaker: Greg Burnham (Epoch AI)
insights.so_what: Continual learning on the job is a missing capability that caps near-term autonomy for AI employees.

insights.claim: Epoch tried simple harnesses, Claude Code, Codex, multi-agent setups and note-taking tools without cracking on-the-fly learning; skills files give quick gains that plateau, and models given detailed human strategy guides do much better but cannot write those guides themselves.
insights.speaker: Greg Burnham (Epoch AI)
insights.so_what: The bottleneck looks like a model-level, not harness-level, problem, which tempers 'agent scaffolding will fix it' theses.

insights.claim: If AI gains fast in-context on-the-fly learning, capabilities could improve much faster than the slow loop of collecting data, doing RL and deploying a new model, and it would raise risk by making deployed systems improve (for example at hacking) after release.
insights.speaker: Greg Burnham (Epoch AI)
insights.so_what: Continual learning is a potential accelerant and a safety wildcard.

insights.claim: Epoch is moving to video games and furniture-assembly (IKEA) tests; Astra and GPT-6 are already pretty good at spotting assembly mistakes from photos, and AI has had little physical-industry impact so far but such skills hint at guided repair applications.
insights.speaker: Greg Burnham (Epoch AI)
insights.so_what: Physical-world guidance (glasses-based assistance) is a plausible next adoption wave before robotics.

themes.theme: Capability thresholds, cyber and alignment risk

insights.claim: Real-world disruption has come from unpredictable thresholds (ChatGPT moment, thinking models, the Claude Code moment letting non-engineers build software) layered on smooth underlying improvement, so tracking mundane capabilities still matters.
insights.speaker: Greg Burnham (Epoch AI)
insights.so_what: Smooth trends underneath can still produce sudden product-market step changes, as in coding.

insights.claim: Burnham cites a Hugging Face hacking incident as an early robust example that alignment is unsolved while capabilities are strong enough to cause problems, and says controlled-setting cyber capabilities are rising smoothly toward a threshold.
insights.speaker: Greg Burnham (Epoch AI)
insights.so_what: Cyber capability is the nearest domain where threshold crossings carry material risk and potential regulatory response.

insights.claim: Burnham frames capability tracking as two jobs: where AI is now for economic utility, and whether the system's dynamics (second derivative, possibly hyperbolic growth) are changing in an alarming way.
insights.speaker: Greg Burnham (Epoch AI)
insights.so_what: Separate level from acceleration when assessing AI progress claims.
